2026/2489.title: FAEST on GPUs: Addressing Field Multiplication as a Bottleneck
2026/2489.abstract: FAEST is a post-quantum signature scheme that combines VOLE-in-the-Head with QuickSilver to prove knowledge of a secret key. It relies on well-established symmetric primitives and offers small public keys, but signing and verification are computationally expensive. We present an NVIDIA GPU implementation of the key-generation core and the QuickSilver procedures OWFProve and OWFVerify for the standard and EM constructions in both s and f variants. Profiling shows that once AES is accelerated by hardware, field multiplication in QuickSilver becomes the largest cost throughout this parameter grid

2026/2488.title: Yoshan: Algebraic-Circuit Co-Synthesis and Search Methodology of Hardware-Efficient S-Boxes
2026/2488.abstract: Choosing a hardware S-box means balancing cryptanalytic strength (differential uniformity δ, linearity L, and algebraic degree) against circuit cost (AND count and AND depth D). Under masking, non-linear gates dominate silicon area, registers, and fresh randomness, while D sets pipeline latency. As a result, automated searches have largely retreated to quadratic permutations (D = 1), whose slow degree growth forces high cipher round counts. We present Yoshan, a co-synthesis engine that optimizes an S-box permutation and its gate-level circuit together across n ∈ {5,6,7,8}. Inside a quality-div

2026/2487.title: A Hybrid BP-SAT Attack on MILENAGE: Combining the Complementary Strengths of Algebraic and Soft-Analytical Side-Channel Attacks
2026/2487.abstract: Profiled side-channel attacks combine noisy leakage predictions with the mathematical relations imposed by the target algorithm to recover secrets from a small number of observations. Two established approaches are algebraic side-channel analysis (ASCA), which encodes leakage predictions and algorithmic relations as a Boolean satisfiability (SAT) problem, and soft-analytical side-channel analysis (SASCA), which performs probabilistic inference over a factor graph using belief propagation (BP). We evaluate both on the AES-based MILENAGE authentication algorithm deployed on USIM cards, targeting

2026/2486.title: Heterogeneous CPU–NPU Implementation of the AIMer Post-Quantum Signature for Low Latency on a Mobile SoC
2026/2486.abstract: Signatures in the MPC-in-the-head paradigm rest only on a symmetric primitive, but their signing is slow, because it computes hash functions and a linear map for every simulated party of every repetition. We show that the Hexagon NPU of Snapdragon SoCs shortens one complete signing operation of AIMer, the MPC-in- the-head signature that the Korean post-quantum cryptography competition selected. Prior work speeds up such signatures on one CPU core, accelerates post-quantum arithmetic on GPUs for batches of operations, and reports only single post-quantum functions for mobile NPUs. Our implement

2026/2485.title: Tulva: Practical Asynchronous Threshold FHE
2026/2485.abstract: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) allows arbitrary computation over encrypted data, but its secret key presents a single point of failure which limits its applications. Threshold FHE patches this gap by distributing the secret key to $K$ parties, requiring a threshold $t \leq K$ of them to cooperate for decryption. We focus on the asynchronous setting where a ciphertext can be decrypted by collecting decryption shares from any $t$ parties who do not need to coordinate or even be online simultaneously. Asynchronous schemes are sought in applications such as privacy-preserving Ethereum Virtual

2026/2484.title: Unveiling the Cost: Gas-Efficient Output-Private Distributed VRFs on Ethereum
2026/2484.abstract: Unbiased and publicly verifiable randomness is a fundamen- tal component of Web3 security, and output-private distributed verifiable random functions (DVRFs) extend this guarantee by keeping the gener- ated randomness hidden from chain observers until the requester chooses to reveal it. Two constructions currently realize output privacy under dif- ferent algebraic regimes: FlexiRand, whose on-chain verification rests on bilinear pairings, and IcyVeil, a pairing-free design whose verification re- duces to a constant number of group operations. While it is folklore that pairing-free verification

2026/2483.title: Uniform Sharing in Multiple Stages: Towards Second-Order Security
2026/2483.abstract: Mitigating Side‑Channel Analysis (SCA) of cryptographic implementations relies heavily on masking schemes; however, achieving efficient and straightforward hardware realizations remains challenging. While Threshold Implementation (TI) provides provable security against glitches in hardware, it incurs significant area overhead due to the large number of shares required to protect non‑linear functions. Successor schemes achieve the same security order with a minimal number of shares, but often rely on a high amount of per‑cycle randomness, especially at higher orders. Recent optimizations such a

2026/2482.title: Edabits Generation with Quasi-Linear Communication Complexity
2026/2482.abstract: The work of (Escudero et al., CRYPTO 2020) introduces the so-called edabits, which are defined as a secret sharing of an integer over an arithmetic domain, together with its bit decomposition secret shared over a binary domain. In the same work, it is shown how edabits can be used to securely evaluate advanced primitives such as comparison, bit decomposition, and truncation, which are essential building blocks in more complex applications such as privacy-preserving machine learning and beyond. Edabits are general and can be defined over any secret-sharing scheme or corruption model. Such flexi

2026/2481.title: Polygero: Proximity Testing From Polynomial Challenges
2026/2481.abstract: We present a new proximity test for Reed--Solomon codes that admits a higher-agreement regime with soundness approaching the field's bit length. All prior work in this area [AHIV2017,BCIKS2020,BCHKS2025] uses the idea of *scalar* batching in which the verifier provides a scalar challenge for each codeword, and the prover must supply a codeword equivalent to the combination, and the verifier tests it at randomly opened columns. 2026/2480.title: Post-Quantum Certificate-Based PSK Provisioning for WireGuard via Mutual TLS, DTLS, and QUIC: Design and Performance Study
2026/2480.abstract: We present an architecture that provides WireGuard’s resistance against future quantum adversaries. By preserving the core protocol, our approach minimizes deployment effort and adds certificate-based identities to WireGuard peers. To achieve Post-Quantum (PQ) resistance, we establish an external mutually authenticated control channel built on the TLS 1.3 handshake and layered on top of TCP, UDP, or QUIC. Its key establishment includes Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM). An auxiliary shared secret is derived from the exported keying material of the resulting session and

2026/2479.title: Committing Security of Forkcipher-based AEAD
2026/2479.abstract: Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) provides confidentiality and integrity, but traditional security notions do not prevent ciphertexts from decrypting correctly under multiple keys. This motivates committing security, which requires ciphertexts to bind to their encryption inputs uniquely. Recent analyses revealed commitment failures in several forkcipher-based AEAD schemes, leaving open the question of whether these failures are inherent to forkciphers or design specific. We provide a comprehensive committing security analysis of existing forkcipher-based AEAD constructions,

2026/2478.title: Hardware-Level Mitigation of Micro-Architectural Leakages in Embedded Processors
2026/2478.abstract: Cryptographic software, with its inherent flexibility and adaptability, has become essential for meeting today’s rapidly evolving security requirements, despite offering lower performance than dedicated hardware accelerators. However, Side-Channel Analysis (SCA) complicates its secure execution on physical hardware, making robust protection a central challenge. While the masking countermeasure offers provable security guarantees in theory, its effectiveness is often undermined by the processor’s micro-architecture. In response, formal adversary models have been adapted to account for micro-arc

2026/2477.title: Secret Sharing Despite Non-Extractable Randomness
2026/2477.abstract: Bosley and Dodis (TCC 2007) proved that a class of imperfect randomness sources that suffices for information-theoretic encryption of messages longer than the logarithm of the key length must admit deterministic extraction of nearly uniform bits, and asked whether the same is true of two-out-of-two secret sharing. Aggarwal, Chung, Obremski, and Ribeiro (TCC 2022) gave a positive answer for schemes that are in addition leakage-resilient or non-malleable; the original question remained open. We answer it in the negative. For every $b\ge2$ we construct a class of flat sources on $\{0,1\}^{b+2}$,

2026/2476.title: On the Hardness of Finding Permutation Automorphisms of Linear Codes
2026/2476.abstract: We study the hardness of finding permutation automorphisms of linear codes. We look into three main problems: $\mathsf{AUT}$, $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$ and $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Count}$ which, respectively, ask to find a non-trivial automorphism, a generating set and the order of the automorphism group. We give polynomial time reductions from $\mathsf{AUT}$ to $\mathsf{ISO}$ (the problem of finding a permutation isomorphism between two linear codes), and from $\mathsf{ISO}$ to $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$ and $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Count}$. This shows that $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$

2026/2475.title: Tamper Sensing Meshes in Payment Terminals and Beyond
2026/2475.abstract: Card Payment Terminals commonly use tamper sensing meshes to deter physical attacks on devices handling sensitive data such as cryptographic keys. Although their use of such meshes is frequently referenced in research literature, the public record contains little research on their construction. Addressing this gap, in this paper we present the first comprehensive analysis of the practical implementation of tamper sensing meshes across a wide range of payment terminals, and some other devices such as ATM key pads and a data center HSM. We provide detailed photos of critical features. Based on o

2026/2474.title: Software-Pipelining The Number Theoretic Transform on Neural Processing Units: A Loop-Fission Methodology
2026/2474.abstract: Lattice-based post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) rely heavily on the number theoretic transform (NTT) for efficient polynomial multiplication. While GPUs and FPGAs have been widely explored for NTT acceleration, neural processing units (NPUs), a rapidly growing class of AI accelerators, remain largely unexplored for cryptographic workloads. In this work, we develop a methodology for accelerating the NTT on NPUs, using AMD’s AI Engine (AIE) architecture as a representative NPU to develop and benchmark it. At its core is manual loop fission, in which large and

2026/2473.title: edaBits in the Exponent (edaBitE) and Issuer-Hiding Blind Signatures from ML-DSA and VOLE-in-the-Head
2026/2473.abstract: Blind signatures let a user obtain a signature by interacting with an issuer that controls the signing key, while the issuer never sees the message. They form the basis of anonymous credentials, which are the centerpiece of privacy-preserving digital identification to be deployed widely in the coming years. Existing plausibly quantum-secure blind signatures rely on bespoke cryptographic constructions, instead of standardized ones. This is dissatisfying from a cryptographic perspective, and also leads to practical issues: secret signing keys are often stored in secure elements, in which case on

2026/2472.title: Nowhere Man: Device Binding for Post-Quantum Anonymous Credentials
2026/2472.abstract: Anonymous credentials are seeing widespread deployment. Notably, the European Commission plans to roll out age-verification solutions based on anonymous credentials by the end of 2026. Similarly, Google open-sourced Longfellow, a zero-knowledge proof system that lifts the standardized mobile Driver License framework into a full-fledged anonymous credentials, and is currently being integrated with Google Wallet. Any secure deployment of anonymous credentials must address two major challenges: 1) provide guarantees against credential sharing, and 2) support proof-of-personhood. The standard appr

2026/2471.title: Connecting Cryptanalytic Distinguishers through Divisibility
2026/2471.abstract: Integral distinguishers can reveal more than a zero-sum property: the number of ones in an output component may be divisible by a high power of $2$, rather than merely being even. To exploit this divisibility, we relate linear, integral, differential-linear, and restricted differential sums through two-way conversions with explicit divisibility guarantees and data complexity, recovering established links as special cases. 2026/2470.title: Refined Application of the XL Algorithm within the Algebraic Approach to the Regular Syndrome Decoding Problem
2026/2470.abstract: The Syndrome Decoding Problem (SDP) is a fundamental mathematical problem underlying code-based cryptography, which is considered a promising candidate for post-quantum cryptography. The Regular Syndrome Decoding Problem (RSDP) is a variant of the SDP in which the error vector follows a specific block-wise structure. Recent developments in RSDP-based cryptographic schemes have led to a wider variety of parameter settings, making it increasingly important to evaluate the complexity of solving the RSDP over a broad range of parameters. One of the main approaches to solving the RSDP is the algebr

2026/2469.title: Accelerating Pollard Rho with GPU Field Arithmetic on NVIDIA Blackwell
2026/2469.abstract: We show how far Pollard rho can be accelerated on current NVIDIA GPUs by rebuilding its field arithmetic around the hardware, with the Certicom challenge ECC2K-130, the Koblitz curve $y^2+xy=x^3+1$ over $\mathbb{F}_{2^{131}}$ with an expected cost of $2^{60.9}$ iterations, as the benchmark. None of the speedup comes from changing the algorithm. 2026/2468.title: FlatMerkle: Logarithmic-Space Inclusion Proofs over a Single Linear Hash Stream
2026/2468.abstract: Merkle trees are the standard way to obtain logarithmic-size, logarithmic-time inclusion proofs over a large dataset, but they require a tree-shaped hash structure distinct from the ordinary, linear (Merkle--Damg\aa rd) hashing that most deployed systems -- including Bitcoin's own transaction and witness hashing -- actually perform. We present FlatMerkle, a construction that achieves the same asymptotic guarantees, $O(\log N)$ proof size and $O(\log N)$ verification time, over a single ordinary linear hash stream, by periodically re-injecting the hash function's own past internal states (``che

2026/2467.title: DPF-SGD: Byzantine-Robust Differentially Private Federated SGD with Exact Optimality Guarantees
2026/2467.abstract: Federated optimization enables collaborative learning over decentralized data but is accompanied by significant privacy risks due to the exchange of model updates. While differential privacy (DP) provides formal protection, optimization accuracy is often degraded, and robustness becomes particularly limited in the presence of Byzantine agents. A Byzantine-robust, differentially private federated SGD algorithm, DPF-SGD, is proposed, in which private step sizes are integrated with a DP noise–decay schedule to regulate gradient updates. 2026/2466.title: Trustless Bitcoin Vaults
2026/2466.abstract: Bitcoin (BTC) is the largest crypto asset, yet the Bitcoin blockchain offers few applications in which BTC can be used. A standard approach to make BTC useful is bridging: BTC is deposited on the Bitcoin chain and a wrapped asset is minted on a chain such as Ethereum, where it can be used in smart contract applications. Unfortunately, all Bitcoin bridges to date require trust assumptions on a centralized party or a committee running the bridge to enable withdrawals of the deposited BTC, including state-of-the-art BitVM bridges. In this paper, we observe that while bridges are application-agnos

2026/2465.title: Snapshots of TEE-Based Encrypted Databases Leak Plaintext Histograms via Dendrochronology
2026/2465.abstract: Arborists use dendrochronology, or the study of tree "growth rings" (as in, the plant), to infer past environmental events. We identify an analogous, exploitable phenomenon in the indexes used by several encrypted databases (EDBs) based on trusted execution environments (TEEs). Such EDBs have been shown to leak the order of indexed values, but not the histogram (or frequency of each value), with respect to a weaker class of snapshot adversaries. 2026/2464.title: A Graph-Based Analysis of Comparability, Scale, and Attribution in Private Transformer Inference
2026/2464.abstract: Rising privacy concerns around large language models have accelerated research in private Transformer inference (PTI). Synthesizing the empirical claims in this line of research, however, is hindered by multi-dimensional cryptographic progress and inconsistent evaluation contracts. In this work, we systematize the field by constructing an empirical graph of 62 PTI systems, mapping system attributes to node features and evaluation compatibility to edges. 2026/2463.title: Tree-BTE: Batched Threshold Encryption using Additive Homomorphism
2026/2463.abstract: Batched threshold encryption (BTE) enables a committee of servers to jointly decrypt any chosen subset of ciphertexts from a large pool, while all remaining ciphertexts stay private. BTE is a key building block for encrypted mempools, where transactions are encrypted until block inclusion to mitigate maximal extractable value (MEV). 2026/2462.title: Hybrid Quantum–Computational Key Distribution with Reduced Assumptions (Short Paper)
2026/2462.abstract: The HM-QCT protocol, presented by Mazzoncini et al. in 2025, uses a unique feature of quantum information to achieve quantum key distribution (QKD) with secret-key rates beyond standard constructions. The protocol has been designed in the hybrid quantum–computational time-lock (QCT) security model which imposes two independent (but related) restrictions on the attacker: (1) a computationally secure encryption scheme which a successful attacker must break within a narrow timeframe and (2) an assumption that the attacker can only store quantum information with low fidelity. 2026/2461.title: Leakage-Resilient Incompressible Cryptography: Constructions and Barriers
2026/2461.abstract: We introduce Leakage-Resilient Incompressible cryptography, which simultaneously addresses two variants of side-channel attacks that have been tackled in theoretical cryptography. Leakage-resilience seeks to provide security against an adversary who learns a part of the secret-key and the entire ciphertext or signature; conversely, incompressible cryptography provides security against an adversary who learns the entire secret-key, but only a part of the ciphertext or signature. However, constructions in either of these security models can fail against an attack in the other model. In this work

2026/2460.title: Cube Attacks with Elimination Strategy: Key Recovery Attacks on Trivium
2026/2460.abstract: In this paper, we present a novel framework for cube attacks named cube attacks with elimination strategy. The core idea is to find specific key conditions and cubes such that their superpolies under these key conditions can be efficiently computed. By recovering these conditional superpolies, we can solve the corresponding equation system and thereby retrieve key information. If a sufficient number of such key conditions can be found, the attack can be extended to a larger key space. To apply this framework in practical attacks, we propose the following techniques. First, we propose a nested

2026/2459.title: Causal Awareness in End-to-End Encrypted Group Messaging
2026/2459.abstract: Chats do not always unfold in a single clear order. Two users may send messages before information about either message reaches the other sender. Such messages are concurrent, but most instant messengers provide no way for users to recognize this relationship. Chen and Fischlin (Eurocrypt 2024) studied this limitation in the two-user setting, showing that Signal does not expose enough information to recover the context in which a message was sent; they proposed a fix. 2026/2458.title: Master-Key Recovery from Internal Activation Leakage in ReLU Realizations of Camellia
2026/2458.abstract: This paper investigates functional correctness and masterkey reconstruction in explicitly constructed rectified linear unit (ReLU) implementations of Camellia-128, Camellia-192, and Camellia-256. Exact neural realizations of Boolean gates, S-box selectors, and bit permutations provide a framework for reproducing Camellia on binary inputs. We present a component-wise correctness argument and report known-answer-test agreement for Camellia-128. 2026/2457.title: On Secure Sorting and Its Application to Privacy-Preserving Graph Pattern Matching
2026/2457.abstract: Sorting in secure computation has been studied almost as long as there have been implementations of multi-party computation (Wang et al., AsiaCCS'10). More recent advances include completely secure implementations (revealing nothing other than the list size) that have used Quicksort (Araki et al., CCS'21) and radix sort (Asharov et al., CCS'22). For the first time, we extensively compare the two variants across a range of parameters and for both honest- and dishonest-majority computation. 2026/2456.title: On the Expected Number of Iterations in ML-DSA Signing: A Complete Accounting of the Rejection Conditions
2026/2456.abstract: FIPS 204 Table 1 gives the expected number of iterations of the ML-DSA signing loop (ML-DSA.Sign_internal, Algorithm 7), citing CRYSTALS-Dilithium Equation (5). 2026/2455.title: CUTS: Chained Uniform-sum Tree Signatures
2026/2455.abstract: Stateful hash-based signatures fail badly when a one-time key signs twice, as happens when the signer's state is lost or rolled back. We study what a second signature reveals in a broad class of hash-based schemes whose key is a tree of hash chains. In this class, a message selects a set of tree nodes that covers every leaf exactly once, together with a position on the chain of each selected node, and the signature reveals the chain values at those positions. 2026/2454.title: Local Leakage Resilience of Shamir Secret Sharing: Below Half Threshold Rate
2026/2454.abstract: We study the local leakage resilience of Shamir secret sharing, where an adversary leaks a bounded number of bits from every share. For $n$ parties and reconstruction threshold $k$ over a prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$ with $p>n$, we prove the following. (1) There is an absolute constant $c_{\mathrm{bh}}<1/2$ such that, for $k\ge c_{\mathrm{bh}}n$, Shamir sharing is resilient to arbitrary one-bit leakage from every share. 2026/2453.title: Revisiting Witness-Succinct UC-lifting Compilers
2026/2453.abstract: Zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge (zkSNARKs) are increasingly used within larger cryptographic protocols, making security under composition essential. Generic compilation to Universal Composability (UC) requires straight-line, black-box extraction while preserving succinctness and controlling prover cost. We introduce verifiable reconstructible straightline codes (VRSCs), a primitive that separates public hiding, transcript-based reconstruction, binding, and proof non-rerandomizability. 2026/2452.title: Genericity in multivariate cryptography
2026/2452.abstract: The results in this paper establish the genericity of some properties of the ideals and varieties generated by UOV public keys, in particular the equidimensionality of the UOV varieties and the radicality of public key ideals. These genericity results justify the various regularity assumptions that are made on polynomial systems of equations arising in the cryptanalysis of UOV and its variants. We also provide examples in the recent literature showing how genericity questions arise in crypt- analysis and why genericity should be taken into consideration when de- signing cryptographic schemes.

2026/2451.title: Extended biprojective APN functions
2026/2451.abstract: Almost perfect nonlinear (APN) functions provide optimal resistance to differential cryptanalysis in characteristic two, and constructing new infinite families inequivalent to the known ones remains an important problem in the study of cryptographic functions. We introduce extended biprojective functions, obtained by augmenting biprojective polynomials with truncated trace terms, and establish a new infinite family of quadratic APN functions. 2026/2450.title: Modulus Operandi: Round-Optimal Modulus Conversion for MPC and Threshold FHE
2026/2450.abstract: In secure multiparty computation (MPC), modulus conversion turns a sharing of a value $x$ modulo $q$ into a sharing of the same value modulo $t$, without leaking anything about $x$. One important application of modulus conversion is in threshold decryption for lattice-based cryptosystems, where a sharing modulo the ciphertext modulus has to be moved to the plaintext modulus before it can be opened. 2026/2449.title: Optimal Threshold Implementations of all bijective 4-bit S-boxes and new Infinite Families
2026/2449.abstract: Threshold implementations (TIs) are now an established class of side-channel countermeasures. Their underlying idea is simple and compelling: under mild, practical assumptions, they provide protection against glitches and allow composability. Yet our understanding of one-stage TIs with a minimal number of shares remains limited, both for cryptographically relevant families—particularly power functions—and for concrete small functions. In particular, until now, except for Feistel-constructions, no optimal TI had been found for families of mathematically well-structured and cryptographically non

2026/2448.title: Breaking First-Order Masked Kyber with Belief Propagation Alone
2026/2448.abstract: We recover the long-term key of a first-order masked Kyber768 implementation on an ARM Cortex-M4 from about 2200 decapsulation power traces, using only authentic ciphertexts that pass ciphertext-validity checks. The secret is freshly shared before every decapsulation, and the attack combines weak second-order leakage from both shares. 2026/2447.title: A methodology to derive security specifications for complex electronic systems
2026/2447.abstract: Modern electronic systems are becoming increas- ingly complex and must satisfy demanding performance, power, and area (PPA) constraints. Consider for instance artificial intelligence chips, aiming at datacenters running LLMs or at automotive perception, which manipulate massive data streams. Beyond performance considerations, these systems must also provide increasingly strong security and dependability guaran- tees. Indeed, when electronic systems are based on chiplets, for instance, the supply chain gets longer and therefore brings a larger number of threats. Also, those systems are very ver

2026/2446.title: Chosen Ciphertext and Trapdoor Secure Public Key Authenticated Encryption with Keyword Search
2026/2446.abstract: For public-key encryption with keyword search (PEKS), chosen-ciphertext attack (CCA) security has been studied in settings where an adversary is allowed to access the test oracle. Notably, the CHK transformation (Canetti, Halevi, and Katz, EUROCRYPT 2004) does not yield CCA-secure PEKS. To address this limitation, Abdalla, Bellare, and Neven (TCC 2010/JoC 2018) proposed a generic construction of CCA-secure PEKS from CCA-secure anonymous and weakly robust identity-based encryption. However, CCA security alone is insufficient to resist keyword-guessing attacks (KGAs) arising from trapdoor leakag

2026/2445.title: A Black-Box Compiler from Static to Dynamic SNARKs
2026/2445.abstract: Succinct Non-Interactive Arguments of Knowledge (SNARKs) for NP allow a prover to prove knowledge of a witness of an NP relation to a verifier with a short proof. The primary goal of a (static) SNARK is to make verification cheap: the proof should be short, and the verifier's work should be minimal. However, recent work has also focused on making SNARKs more prover-efficient: cheap verification should ideally not come at the cost of large prover overhead. 2026/2444.title: Extending the Schur--Macaulay Framework for UOV Attacks via Truncated Polynomial Algebras
2026/2444.abstract: Building on the ideal-inclusion framework of Ding, Li, and Tao, we reformulate and extend the Schur--Macaulay approach of Merz and Ran using multigraded $p$-truncated polynomial algebras over arbitrary finite fields. The construction admits a reconciliation interpretation involving multiple oil vectors. Combining divided powers with transfer relation spaces, we derive quotient-dimension criteria for recovering graded components of the hidden oil-space ideal. 2026/2443.title: Worst-Case Hardness for Succinct and Decomposed Learning with Errors
2026/2443.abstract: The succinct LWE (CRYPTO~'24) and decomposed LWE (CRYPTO~'25) assumptions are two recently introduced variants of the celebrated LWE problem, known to imply the existence of numerous new cryptographic primitives. Yet, the hardness of these problems has thus far remained poorly understood, since there is no known reduction to LWE. In this work, we study these lattice problems from a foundational perspective. 2026/2442.title: Faster generic CCA secure KEM transformation using encrypt-then-MAC
2026/2442.abstract: ML-KEM is a lattice-based IND-CCA secure key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) standardized by NIST in FIPS 203. ML-KEM achieves chosen-ciphertext security by applying the Fujisaki-Okamoto (FO) transformation to an IND-CPA secure public key encryption (PKE) scheme. 2026/2441.title: Nobody Will Read the Lean: A Case for High-Level Cryptographic Languages
2026/2441.abstract: In September 2026, an AI produced a Lean proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in eleven days, and AI provers have started on cryptography. Within a few years, an AI may hand you a machine-checked proof that Signal is secure. You won't need to read it, because Lean will have checked every step. What Lean can't check is whether the theorem says what you think it says. That depends on its definitions, which the AI will also have written at length for that one proof. This already happens. 2026/2440.title: Staggered Instruction-Fetch Duplication: A Lightweight Processor-Level Countermeasure Against Fault Injection
2026/2440.abstract: Fault attacks exploit transient hardware faults to bypass software-level security checks in embedded processors. Processor-level redundancy can detect such faults, but duplicating the whole processor is costly for resource-constrained devices. This paper proposes Staggered Instruction-Fetch Duplication (SIFD), a lightweight processor-level countermeasure based on instruction-fetch redundancy. SIFD fetches each instruction twice in consecutive cycles, while fetching two different instructions in every fetch cycle. This staggered schedule detects inconsistent fetch results without full processor

2026/2439.title: Efficient Vectorized Implementation of MQOM
2026/2439.abstract: Post-quantum signature schemes require efficient implementations to be viable in practice. MQOM, a third-round candidate in NIST’s additional call for digital signatures, is a promising target for SIMD optimization. This work leverages a transpose-enabled paired-matrix trick to develop a vectorized implementation of MQOM v2.1, corresponding to the Round-2 specification, with reduced wasted SIMD work and memory traffic. We evaluate MQOM v2.1 on Arm NEON, x86 AVX2, and x86 AVX-512, covering key generation, signing, verification, and memory; peak dynamic memory falls by up to 39.43%. We also incl

2026/2438.title: Censorship Resistance in Credential Systems and Application to the EUDI Wallet
2026/2438.abstract: Privacy-preserving credential systems typically focus on data protection during the presentation phase, overlooking potential privacy threats during issuance. A malicious issuer could use the non-minimal information it obtains to deny issuance selectively. Such a denial, going beyond the eligibility policy, is a form of censorship. In this work, we revisit the security of anonymous credential systems to protect users from malicious issuers during credential issuance. We first highlight the limitations of existing definitions and introduce a security model capturing censorship resistance. Next,

2026/2437.title: Confidential Error-Correcting Codes
2026/2437.abstract: We introduce Confidential Error-correcting Codes (CECs), a new cryptographic primitive that enables reliable decoding from perturbed codewords while preserving message confidentiality. We formalize this primitive through three security properties: confidentiality, robustness, and soundness. To realize this goal, we develop a general framework for constructing CECs based on a Randomness-Security Separation (RSS) structure, which first encodes a nonce to introduce randomness and then masks the encoded payload with a pseudorandom function. Based on our RSS framework, we instantiate CECs, called C

2026/2436.title: Threshold BARGs with Statistical Soundness: Weighted Threshold Encryption without Obfuscation
2026/2436.abstract: Non-interactive batch arguments (BARGs) for $\mathsf{NP}$ enable proving the validity of $k$ $\mathsf{NP}$ statements with a proof whose size is independent of $k$. Threshold BARGs are a natural generalization that enables proving that at least $t$ out of $k$ statements are valid. Unfortunately, existing threshold BARG constructions have the drawback that the size of the common reference string (CRS) grows polynomially with $k$. This is the case even when the statements have a short description (e.g., when considering index languages). Moreover, other than constructions based on indistinguisha

2026/2435.title: TenseUp: Doubly-Efficient Lookup Arguments from Tensor Codes and Applications to Dynamic SNARKs
2026/2435.abstract: Doubly-Efficient Lookup Arguments are specialized argument systems that enable succinctly proving the correctness of a batch of $k$ lookup accesses to a large table $\textbf{x}$ in time proportional to $k$ and sublinear in $|\textbf{x}|$. All existing such schemes suffer from one of the following limitations. Either they rely on elliptic-curve-based assumptions for their security, hence they are not secure against quantum adversaries, or are rather impractical, as they rely on algorithms for fast polynomial evaluations (that are mostly of theoretical interest), or operate over fields of small

2026/2434.title: Witness-Succinct UC-Secure SNARKs with Weaker Trust Assumptions
2026/2434.abstract: Zero-knowledge Succinct Non-Interactive Arguments of Knowledge (zkSNARKs) are foundational cryptographic primitives enabling privacy-preserving and verifiable computation. However, most existing zkSNARK constructions rely on strong trust assumptions—typically a fully trusted setup—which undermines their applicability in adversarial or decentralized environments. Although transparent zkSNARKs remove this assumption, they typically do not satisfy strong composability guarantees such as Universal Composability (UC). In this work, we present the first framework for constructing UC-secure zkSNARKs

2026/2433.title: Succinct Arguments with (almost) Minimal Time and Space Overheads from Symmetric-Key Primitives
2026/2433.abstract: We construct public-coin, succinct, zero-knowledge interactive arguments for NP relations decided by time-$T$, space-$S$ random-access machines. Assuming the existence of collision-resistant hash functions, our arguments give a frontier of tradeoffs between prover time and space, and proof size. We follow the streaming PIOP+PCS framework of Block et al. (TCC 2020, CRYPTO 2021), reducing the problem of constructing time- and space-efficient arguments to time- and space-efficient streaming multilinear polynomial commitment schemes (MLPCS). We develop two code-based streaming MLPCS inspired by Br

2026/2432.title: Lattice Bingo: Asynchrony and One-Shot Adaptivity in Verifiable Secret Sharing via Erasure Code Commitments
2026/2432.abstract: Asynchronous verifiable secret sharing (AVSS) allows a dealer to distribute a secret among parties while preserving privacy and consistent reconstruction, despite Byzantine faults and arbitrary message delays. It is a fundamental building block for Byzantine agreement, distributed key generation, and secure multiparty computation. Packed AVSS protocols share many secrets together to reduce communication per secret. The best known AVSS protocols achieve quadratic communication while sharing linearly many secrets. In particular, Bingo (Abraham et al., CRYPTO 2023) shares a batch of $\Theta(k)$ s

2026/2431.title: Flying, Not Floating: Precise Fixed-Point Falcon on Embedded Processors
2026/2431.abstract: The Falcon digital signature scheme, under standardization as FN-DSA, requires real-number arithmetic during signing, with its security dependent on numerical precision. Recently, De Almeida Braga et al. (CRYPTO 2026) showed that Falcon-512 can sign in 64.64 fixed-point arithmetic on 64-bit hosts. In this work, we present the first fixed-point FN-DSA signer for microcontrollers, using 32.64 arithmetic in constant-time Cortex-M4 assembly for Falcon-512 and Falcon-1024. Although a straightforward fixed-point implementation is less precise than double precision, our new techniques successfully re

2026/2430.title: Distinguishers for the Squeezing of the Alternating Sponge and Duet
2026/2430.abstract: Recently, the Institute of Commercial Cryptography Standards (ICCS) launched the Next Generation Commercial Cryptographic Algorithm Program (NGCC), which includes a standardization process for cryptographic hash functions. In this note, we analyze the mode of operation of Duet, one of the hash-function candidates. Duet is a permutation-based hash function directly inspired by the Alternating Sponge (ASP). Both constructions use two permutations on $b=r+c$ bits, split into an outer part of $r$ bits and an inner part of $c$ bits. We first present a distinguisher against ASP requiring $\mathcal{O

2026/2429.title: Rapid mixing in superspecial isogeny graphs
2026/2429.abstract: We prove expansion properties of superspecial isogeny graphs in dimension $g \geq 2$, including arbitrary level structure. In particular, we provide explicit bounds for the spectral gap, and a fine characterization of obstructions created by level structures (disconnectedness and periodicity). Without the level structure (the only case which was previously studied), our bounds dramatically improve the state of the art. These isogenies in dimension greater than one have become increasingly important in isogeny-based cryptography, and previous works have already conjectured consequences of their

2026/2428.title: Beyond-Birthday MAC Security for Encrypted Wegman-Carter and EWCDMD
2026/2428.abstract: At CRYPTO 2016, Cogliati and Seurin proposed EWCDM as a nonce-based MAC construction making two block cipher calls and one almost-XOR-universal (AXU) hash evaluation and achieving beyond-birthday-bound (BBB) security. They noticed that a simplified variant of EWCDM named Encrypted Wegman--Carter (EWC) admits a birthday distinguishing attack. Later, at CRYPTO 2017, Mennink and Neves proposed EWCDMD, the dual of EWCDM, as a new candidate BBB-secure MAC, but at EUROCRYPT 2020 Nandi proposed a birthday distinguishing attack against EWCDMD. However, the distinguishing attacks did not yield forgerie

2026/2427.title: RM-KLPT: Algebraic Pathfinding for Superspecial Abelian Surfaces with Maximal Real Multiplication
2026/2427.abstract: The isogeny graphs of superspecial abelian surfaces with maximal real multiplication were first studied by Charles, Goren, and Lauter in 2009, when they constructed the RM-CGL hash function on these graphs and proved that they are Ramanujan. As a consequence, these graphs enjoy optimal expansion properties, which are either absent or difficult to establish in other higher-dimensional isogeny graphs. In this paper, we take a closer look at these graphs from a cryptographic perspective, and attempt to demonstrate that they are the natural generalization of the supersingular $\ell$-isogeny graph

2026/2426.title: Provably Subexponential Algorithms for Bounded-Error LWE with Few Samples
2026/2426.abstract: We show that a variant of the Wagner/BKW-style algorithm for LWE of Kirchner and Fouque [KF15] solves decision and search LWE with secrets of size $n$ over prime moduli $q=n^{\kappa+o(1)}$, for any fixed $\kappa>0$, with errors bounded by $\exp((\ln n)^{o(1)})$, in time $2^{O(n/\ln\ln n)}$ given $n+O(n/\ln\ln n)$ original samples. Further, if each coordinate of the secret is also bounded by $\exp((\ln n)^{o(1)})$, the same time bound holds with errors bounded by $n^{o(1)}$ and only $O(n/\ln\ln q)$ samples. 2026/2425.title: Sample-Preserving Search-to-Decision Reduction for Noisy Linear Equations over Large Moduli
2026/2425.abstract: The Noisy Linear Equations problem involves finding the solution to a random linear system over a finite field given noisy evaluations. This is a generalisation of various learning problems widely used in cryptography, including Learning with Errors (LWE), Learning with Rounding (LWR), and Learning Parity with Noise (LPN). We present a new sample-preserving search-to-decision reduction for Noisy Linear Equations that has complexity $\mathrm{poly}(n,m,\log q, q/\sigma)$, where $n$ is the dimension of the secret, $m$ is the number of samples, $q$ is the modulus, and $\sigma$ is the magnitude of

2026/2424.title: Counterexamples to Beyond-Johnson Proximity Gaps over Binary Fields
2026/2424.abstract: Many hash-based proof systems check that committed words are close to Reed–Solomon codewords by testing one random combination of them. Their soundness analysis uses a *proximity gap*: if the combination agrees with a codeword on many positions, so do the original words, on the same positions, except for a few *exceptional* challenges. Such gaps are known above the Johnson threshold, about $\sqrt\rho$ for rate $\rho$, and extending them below it would shrink proofs. Recent work does so in large characteristic, but not for the additive domains used over binary fields, where some of the fastest

2026/2423.title: Magnetar: High-speed post-quantum RV64 zkVM from standard hashes
2026/2423.abstract: We describe the design, implementation, and experimental evaluation of Magnetar, a transparent proof system for RV64I program executions (i.e., a zkVM). Magnetar is the first zkVM to simultaneously satisfy the following three properties: 1. General-purpose proving. Magnetar proves programs compiled to the general-purpose RV64I ISA. An implementation of the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) written in Rust or Go can therefore run inside Magnetar, yielding a zkEVM for proving executions of existing EVM smart contracts. 2. Hash-based, post-quantum security. Magnetar’s cryptographic security is roote

2026/2422.title: Verifiable Computation on Encrypted Data from Homomorphic Encryption over Random Encodings
2026/2422.abstract: Verifiable Computation on Encrypted Data (vCOED) enables clients to outsource computation while providing both privacy and integrity. A promising vCOED paradigm is blind proofs, which use homomorphic encryption (HE) to evaluate verifiable computation (VC) proofs on encrypted data. Despite their efficiency, blind proofs do not provide strong client privacy: a malicious server can exploit reaction attacks to learn information about the client's inputs, intermediate values or final outputs. Our work addresses this limitation by introducing Homomorphic Encryption over Random Encodings (HERE). We f

2026/2421.title: Efficient Unbiasable Verifiable Random Functions via (Non-)Black-Box Reductions
2026/2421.abstract: We present conceptually simple and practically efficient constructions of a verifiable random function (VRF) that fulfills strong notions of unbiasability recently introduced by Giunta and Stewart (Eurocrypt 2024). Unbiasability is a crucial property for many applications of VRFs such as leader election in proof-of-stake blockchains. The only previous constructions provide heuristic security in the random oracle model or rely on the decisional Diffie–Hellman assumption with preprocessing which incurs significant overhead. 2026/2420.title: Provable Subexponential Algorithms for Module-SIS and Module-LWE
2026/2420.abstract: Ducas, Engelberts and Loyer (CRYPTO 2025) turned Wagner's generalized birthday algorithm into a provable subexponential-time Gaussian sampler for unstructured short integer solutions. Recent preprints of Han, Gao and Hu, and of Chen, Jiang, Wang and Zhang, obtain low-sample decision learning-with-errors algorithms from this framework. We extend it to module matrices over power-of-two cyclotomic rings, for every residue degree of the prime modulus. For fixed module ranks $k,\ell\ge1$, let $n=kd$, $m=(k+\ell)d$, and suppose $\ln(q/\sqrt n)=(\ln n)^{b+o(1)}$. For every fixed $b,c,\xi>0$, we solve

2026/2419.title: Optimal Statistical Oblivious RAM and Search Tree in the External-Memory Model
2026/2419.abstract: Oblivious RAM (ORAM) allows a trusted client to access (encrypted) data stored in untrusted memory, such that the access patterns reveal nothing about the data or the queries. It is well-known that any ORAM scheme must suffer from a logarithmic overhead. More precisely stated, each request must incur $\Omega(\log_B N)$ block transfers on average, where $N$ is the size of the logical memory and $B$ is the block size of the oblivious implementation. Moreover, the same lower bound extends to oblivious Search Trees (ST). For upper bounds, however, we have been long stuck with a $(\log_B N)^2$ curs

2026/2418.title: Individual Cryptography from Iterated Squaring
2026/2418.abstract: Individual cryptography (Dziembowski et al. Crypto'23) and complete knowledge (Kelkar et al. CCS'24) aim at constructing protocols that ensure that some individual party must know a secret value in the clear, and so the computation cannot have been “outsourced” to an MPC computation. Two central primitives are proofs of complete (or individual) knowledge, which enforce that some party actually knows the secret witness, and secret sharing with snitching, which enforces that whenever the secret is reconstructed, some party must learn a certificate of this fact. The instantiations proposed by bot

2026/2417.title: Unpredictability from Parity: Understanding Linear Correctors for Markovian Sources
2026/2417.abstract: Linear correctors reduce the bias of random bits via parity (XOR), but their guarantees are known mostly for independent bits, an assumption violated by many physical entropy sources. We give a general, exact formula for the parity bias of dependent bits from a (hidden, possibly non-homogeneous) Markov chain, as a product of twisted transfer kernels. Under next-bit unpredictability, i.e. conditional bias at most $\beta$, the decay is governed by $\beta$ itself: sharp for a one-bit context, $|\mathrm{bias}|\le\beta^{\lceil n/2\rceil}$, and \emph{near-optimal} for an $m$-bit context, within a fa

2026/2416.title: New Constructions of Quadratic and Cubic Permutations Admitting Optimal Threshold Implementations
2026/2416.abstract: Side-channel attacks can uncover sensitive data by analyzing information leakages of cryptographic hardware devices caused by the power consumption, timing, electromagnetic, glitches, etc. Threshold implementation (TI), introduced by Nikova et al. in 2006, was proposed to resist differential power analysis side-channel attack on hardware implementations of block ciphers and eliminate information leakage due to glitches. 2026/2415.title: The Power of Multislices in Monotone Computation
2026/2415.abstract: Motivated by recent constructions and barriers in secret sharing, we study multislice functions. These functions, parametrized by a width parameter $w$, take the value 0 on inputs of Hamming weight below a base value $k$, 1 on inputs of weight above $k+w$, and are monotone in between. We first investigate formulas over multislice gates, which generalize the formulas over slices model (Applebaum et al., TOCT 2026). 2026/2414.title: Reverse-Bleichenbacher: Bleichenbacher Attacks are Practical Again
2026/2414.abstract: Bleichenbacher's 1998 padding oracle attack against RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 has resurfaced repeatedly over the past decades, especially in TLS. Although modern browsers prefer TLS 1.3, many servers and clients still permit RSA key exchange for backward compatibility, enabling active network attackers to decrypt recorded sessions. Still, practical man-in-the-middle attacks remain challenging. The classical attack narrows the plaintext interval from the top down, spending many queries on secret-independent padding bytes before reaching the PreMasterSecret in the low-order 46 bytes of the RSA plaintext.

2026/2413.title: Fast Polynomial Arithmetic in the Exponent without Roots of Unity
2026/2413.abstract: In cryptographic algorithms based on groups in which the discrete logarithm is supposed to be hard, it is frequent to perform polynomial arithmetic in the exponent of group elements. This old technique has become a critical operation in many recent advanced protocols, mostly related to commitments and zero-knowledge proofs, where polynomials of high degrees are involved. Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) techniques in the exponent are often implemented to gain speed. However, they require roots of unity to exist in the field GF(q) where q is the order of the group. 2026/2412.title: Barely Sublinear RAM-FHE from Plain LWE
2026/2412.abstract: Fully Homomorphic Encryption for RAM programs (RAM-FHE), introduced by Hamlin, Holmgren, Weiss, and Wichs (Crypto 2019), allows a server to evaluate a RAM program on encrypted data at a per-step cost sublinear in the memory size $N$, whereas standard FHE must read the entire memory for every memory access. In a celebrated work, Lin, Mook, and Wichs (STOC 2023) gave the first, and to date the only, construction from a concrete assumption, namely Ring-LWE. In this work, we construct a RAM-FHE scheme from plain LWE that evaluates each step of a RAM program in $o(N/\log N)$ time. While the scheme

2026/2411.title: Average-Case Hardness of Lattice Problems in Special Genera of Fixed Rank
2026/2411.abstract: The distinguishing variant $\Delta$LIP of the Lattice Isomorphism Problem underlies the security proofs of a growing family of lattice-based schemes. As the special genus is the strongest efficiently computable invariant of a lattice, such a proof may replace the lattice used by the scheme with a random lattice of the same genus. This raises the question of how hard lattice problems actually are on such random lattices. We answer it, under GRH, with a worst-case to average-case reduction inside any special genus $\mathcal{G}$ of Hermitian lattices of fixed rank $r \geq 2$ over a cyclotomic fie

2026/2410.title: KIFA: Kernel-based Integral Fault Analysis on GIFT-Family Ciphers
2026/2410.abstract: We present KIFA (Kernel-based Integral Fault Analysis), an integral fault attack framework that mines its balanced properties with the kernel-based miner of Hwang et al. in place of Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP). The miner handles only small input structures fixed in advance, and a fault model provides exactly such structures. For DEFAULT, we present attacks at fault penetration (FP) $9$ under a random-position nibble fault and FP $10$ under a random-position byte fault, beyond the prior best integral fault attack at FP $8$. They leave a single master-key candidate under the simple k

2026/2409.title: Mercury: Fuzzy Private Set Intersection with Communication and Computation Logarithmic in the Threshold
2026/2409.abstract: Private Set Intersection (PSI) allows two mutually distrusting parties to compute the intersection of their sets without revealing any additional information and has found numerous applications. The approximate matching required by various applications has led to the development of Fuzzy PSI (FPSI), a variant of PSI that identifies approximate intersection elements under a public distance threshold \(\delta\). Reducing computation and communication costs remains an important challenge for FPSI. In this paper, we present a new FPSI protocol, called Mercury, which achieves logarithmic computatio

2026/2408.title: Separating One-Way Functions from Verifiable Delay Functions
2026/2408.abstract: Timed cryptography captures computations that inherently require a prescribed amount of time, even in the presence of parallelism, and has emerged as a central notion due to its broad applications in both practice and theory. A natural question is how timed cryptographic primitives relate to traditional cryptography, in particular to primitives in Minicrypt. Guan and Montgomery (CRYPTO 2024) show that sequential functions do not imply one-way functions (OWFs) via black-box reductions. Their result, however, leaves open whether adding public verifiability (a substantially stronger requirement)

2026/2407.title: Language Modeling is Monotone Compression
2026/2407.abstract: A long-standing hypothesis in artificial intelligence and neuroscience posits that intelligence is closely related to compression: the ability to compress information efficiently intuitively reflects capacities associated with intelligence and learning. Indeed, recent experimental works verify this intuition by showing connections between the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and their ability as compressors: for instance, Deletang et al. (ICLR'24) demonstrate that LLMs can be used as powerful compressors, and Huang et al. (COLM'24) show that the compression ability of LLMs is highl

2026/2406.title: Time-Space Tradeoffs For Probabilistic Proofs
2026/2406.abstract: Many recent constructions of probabilistic proofs achieve fast proving times but have high space complexity (much higher than that of the computation being proved). Empirically this arises due to the fact that error-correcting codes, a key ingredient of such constructions, suffer from limiting time-space tradeoffs. It remained open, however, whether such time-space tradeoffs exist for proofs themselves. 2026/2405.title: Game-Theoretically Fair Coin Toss from Random Walk Against $n-1$ Corruptions
2026/2405.abstract: Coin-tossing protocols allow mutually distrustful parties to generate trusted randomness. While strong fairness is impossible against a corrupted majority, Chung et al. (2018) introduced cooperative-strategy-proof (CSP) fairness for multi-party coin tossing, under the assumption that each party gets utility only when the outcome matches its public preference. CSP-fairness ensures that no PPT adversary can increase the expected joint utility of the corrupted parties through deviation. 2026/2404.title: The Geometry of Collusion Leakage in Inner-Product Functional Encryption
2026/2404.abstract: Inner-product functional encryption (IPFE) allows the holder of a functional key for a vector $y$ to learn $\langle x,y\rangle$ from an encryption of $x$, and nothing more. Keys, however, accumulate: a coalition holding sufficiently many independent keys recovers the plaintext. We model each institution by the span $W_i\leq\F_q^n$ of its authorized key vectors and show that a coalition $I$ determines the plaintext exactly modulo $(\sum_{i\in I}W_i)^\perp$; for a uniform plaintext it learns exactly $\dim\sum_{i\in I}W_i$ field symbols. 2026/2403.title: Practical and Efficient MPC from FHE, without ZKPoKs
2026/2403.abstract: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) enables one to implement low-round and low-communication complexity Multi-Party Computation (MPC) which is secure in the static malicious corruption model. By expanding on an idea presented in the full version of the FHE-based MPC protocol of Smart (IMA, 2023), we show how to completely remove the need for Zero-Knowledge Proofs-of-Knowledge in that protocol. This simplification makes the final security proof of the MPC protocol much simpler, and more modular. The new protocol makes use of an FHE scheme with an encrypted PRF functionality, and in addition to o

2026/2402.title: Revisiting Lattice-based Blind Signatures Again
2026/2402.abstract: We show an attack on a lattice-based blind signature proposed in Crypto'20. Formally it is a linear hash function based framework with a lattice-based instantiation. We first notice a bug in their security proof of blindness, which is overlooked these years. Then, we develop an attack under the honest key and the honest-but-curious signer setting against the blindness notion of the schemes by exploiting the coorelations between the leaves of the tree. We also discuss how to repair the scheme.

2026/2401.title: New infinite families of APN functions from the switching construction in even dimension
2026/2401.abstract: We present the first new infinite family of APN functions obtained by applying the switching construction to a known family since the introduction of the Budaghyan-Carlet-Leander family in 2009. Our construction is also the first example of an infinite APN family obtained via the switching construction from an infinite family of non-power functions. More generally, we study families of APN functions that can be obtained from the Budaghyan-Helleseth-Kaleyski family by the addition of carefully selected perturbation terms. 2026/2400.title: Simple Byzantine Lattice Agreement in $O(\frac{\log f}{\log \log f})$ Rounds
2026/2400.abstract: Lattice agreement is a relaxed version of the standard consensus problem: correct processes need not decide the same value, but their decisions must be ``comparable''. Namely, every process proposes a value from a join semi-lattice, and correct processes decide values that (1) lie on a single chain, (2) include their own proposals, and (3) include nothing beyond what was proposed. Lattice agreement has important practical applications, as it underpins atomic snapshot objects and replicated state machines with commutative operations. 2026/2399.title: A Note on Extractable Witness Encryption in Generic Groups
2026/2399.abstract: Hair and Sahai (arXiv:2609.18275v1) have recently proposed a construction of witness encryption for NP satisfying semantic security. In this note we observe that this recent witness-encryption construction is unconditionally extractable in the generic group model. This yields a construction of extractable witness encryption without assuming subexponential soundness of SNARGs, in contrast to the recent work of Jin (ePrint 2026/2063), which requires this assumption. The result in this note, moreover, complements the concurrent work of Chen and Vaikuntanathan (ePrint 2026/2346), who show the same

2026/2398.title: Note on Extractability of PST Polynomial Commitment Scheme
2026/2398.abstract: A recent work by Belohorec et al. (Crypto, 2025) shows that the well-known PST multivariate polynomial commitment scheme is black-box extractable under falsifiable assumptions. They show that a minimally modified (extended) PST is extractable under an assumption ARSDH($n$), and that the canonical PST is extractable under an assumption GARSDH($n$). Both of these assumptions are new and more specialized than the original ARSDH assumption proposed by Lipmaa et al. 2026/2397.title: Hashing Beats Trees: Practical Oblivious Dictionaries in SGX
2026/2397.abstract: Oblivious RAM (ORAM) is a powerful cryptographic primitive that hides both the contents of outsourced data and the access pattern to the data. However, it offers only a restrictive array-based interface. A principal obstacle to its deployment is building an efficient oblivious dictionary upon it. To build such a dictionary, the state-of-the-art layers an oblivious AVL tree over ORAM, avoids an expensive local position map, but forces every operation to traverse a full root-to-leaf path, costing $\Theta(\log n)$ ORAM accesses. We show this trade-off to be suboptimal, particularly when deployed

2026/2396.title: Hide Now, Trace Later: Retrospective Attribution in Issuer-Hiding Credentials
2026/2396.abstract: Attribute-based credentials (ABCs) enable privacy-preserving authentication by allowing users to prove statements about certified attributes without revealing unnecessary information. However, while ABCs hide undisclosed attributes, the credential verification process inherently reveals the issuer's identity, which can leak contextual information such as a user's nationality or residency. Issuer-hiding ABCs address this by concealing the issuer during verification, but introduce a critical accountability problem: if an issuer is compromised or acts maliciously, previously accepted presentation

2026/2395.title: The Price of Privacy: Randomness Complexity of Graph-Based Multi-Secret Sharing
2026/2395.abstract: We study the randomness required to share possibly correlated secret bits among parties connected by a graph. A dealer places shares on the edges so that each party can recover its own secret from its incident shares and learn nothing about the others beyond what its own secret reveals. Anilkumar et al. completely determined the minimum randomness required for three binary secrets. We extend this study to four secrets and obtain results for arbitrary numbers of secrets on general graphs.
